newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand Post -- from dinsosaur to exporter.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand Post -- from dinsosaur to exporter.

text.p: New Zealand Post was labelled a basket case 10 years ago.
Now, it has not only put its house in order but said on Wednesday it wants to teach the world how it did it.
It sees postal services as a last frontier of deregulation and, in conjunction with New Zealand utilities investor Infratil International, has begun a campaign to export services.
Last week they were part of a consortium shortlisted in a bid for the privatisation of Argentina's postal firm ENCOTESA.
"...Postal infrastructure is possibly the last unreformed infrastructure service," NZ Post chief executive Elmar Toime told reporters at a profit briefing.
He said failure to reform postal services in developing countries would restrain economic reform. An efficient post service was a vital cog in democratic machinery.
"If an economy is moving forward, in the sheer act of invoicing people for electricity, telephones or cellphones, you have to have that infrastructure in place," he said.
Despite the relative sophistication of the Argentine economy, its people post only 15 letters a year each against 280 in New Zealand and about 600 in the United States.
NZ Post believes it can get into the advisory services in a much bigger way, advising countries not only how to deregulate but how to expand postal markets.
"We see very bright prospects in this area," said Toime, adding that such business was also profitable. Revenue in the 1996/97 year was around NZ$4 million.
NZ Post is currently advising the South African government on how to update its electoral enrolment programme.
In 1987, the Labour government transformed the state-owned postal service into a State-Owned Enterprise.
The government was accused of making the move as precursor to privatisation but then deputy prime minister Sir Geoffrey Palmer said it could not be given away, such were its losses.
NZ Post is so proud of its achievements since then it has commissioned a 10 year anniversary book called 'Reining in the Dinosaur'.
On Wednesday, it reported net profit of NZ$47.7 million in the year to March 31.
While the profit was well down on the $75.2 million reported in 1996, the government has been heavily reducing its capital. It paid a dividend in 1996/97 of NZ$113.6 million.
NZ Post's debt to debt plus equity ratio has risen to 38 percent from 27 percent last year but even on the reduced profit is still returning a healthy 25 percent on shareholders' funds.
To compete with the ever increasing threat of greater use of telephone, fax and internet services, NZ Post last year cut the cost of a standard letter to 40 cents from 45 cents.
It says the price cut has been instrumental in allowing mail volumes to increase despite competition from electronic services.
In April, the government announced it was deregulating the letter market by removing NZ Post's monopoly.
NZ Post said it was ready for that move, although it expects it to impact on profitability, holding earnings to current levels despite volume growth in all its markets.
"The company supports the decision to deregulate. We don't doubt competition brings its challenges," Toime said.
"But we are confident about perfoming in a deregulated market."
